title: Code health: dead code, test gaps, duplicates, security

story: A tool that finds unused code is easy to run. Point knip, a tool that lists unused files and exports in a TypeScript project, at our frontend and it prints a long list in a few seconds. Delete everything on the list and the build may still pass, and then a page that loads a widget by name, with a dynamic import that knip cannot follow, breaks in production.

So the list is a list of suspects, not of facts. A routine that cleans the codebase every night has to tell the two apart, and it has to produce a PR that a reviewer can approve in minutes, not a 400-file deletion nobody dares to merge.
hook.question: How does a code-health routine turn a tool's list of suspects into a small change that is safe to approve?

p: Every code-health routine has the same shape, whether it removes dead code, adds missing tests, merges duplicates or bumps a vulnerable package. These routines are the same agent as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, started by a weekly or daily schedule instead of a ticket. A finder, usually an ordinary tool, lists candidates. Verifiers, read-only helper sessions that may run many at a time inside the VM, check each candidate and either prove it or drop it. Then one writer session makes a small change, and the PR shows the proof for every item.

The split is on purpose. Reading is where extra agents help: ten verifiers can each check one candidate at the same time, and none of them can break anything, because they cannot write. Writing is where extra agents hurt, because two writers in one codebase step on each other. So there is always exactly one writer, and the PR stays small: at most 10 deleted items, at most 5 new tests, or one merge proposal a week.

For dead frontend code the finder is knip. It starts from entry files, such as Next.js pages, stories, unit tests and e2e specs, follows every import, and reports what it never reached. That is a good finder and a bad judge, because some code is reached in ways no import graph shows: a dynamic import built from a string, a component named in a config, a page object used only by an e2e spec, an export of our shared @r/libs package used by another app.

So each candidate goes to a verifier with a checklist of exactly those places, and the rule is simple: anything the verifier cannot prove unused is dropped, not deleted. A dropped item costs nothing; it stays one more week. A wrong deletion costs a broken page and the team's trust in the routine. The charter adds a matching wall: the dead-code routine has never: add_code, so the false-heal check rejects any diff that adds code instead of only removing it.

p: knip only knows what its entry files reach, so the configuration decides how good the list is. The entries name everything the framework or the tools load by convention, and the project globs name the files to check. The frontend guild reviews this file and runs knip by hand until false positives are rare, before the routine ever starts.

read.h: The same shape, three more times
p: The backend dead-code remover uses vulture, a Python tool that reports unused code with a confidence score, starting strict at 80. Its verifier knows where Django hides usage: URL configs, the admin, signals, Celery tasks called by name, DRF hooks, management commands, settings strings and the public SDK, which is never touched.

The test-gap routine copies the roles of a published Meta system called ACH. One helper plants a small realistic bug, a mutant, in recently changed code that no test covers; another drops mutants that do not change behaviour; the one writer adds a test, which is kept only if it fails on its planted bug and passes on clean code. The duplicates sweep lists near-copies with jscpd, lets read-only judges decide whether two copies really change for the same reason, and proposes one merge a week. The security fixer takes a scanner finding that has a fixed release, bumps the package with the upgrade fixers' pipeline, and proves with the scanner, before and after, that the finding is gone. Four routines, one shape: find, prove, one small write.

lab.title: Prove or drop
needs: npm (npx downloads knip the first time)
lab.goal: Run knip on a tiny project, prove or drop each candidate with a verifier, and delete only what is proven.

guess.q: knip says src/widgets/chart.ts is unused, but src/index.ts loads widgets with import(`./widgets/${name}.ts`). What should the routine do with chart.ts?

options.text: Delete it: knip followed every import.
options.why: knip cannot follow an import built from a string. Deleting it breaks the page at run time.

options.text: Drop it from the list: the verifier finds a string reference, so it is not proven unused.
options.why: Anything the verifier cannot prove unused stays, at no cost.

options.text: Ask the writer to rewrite the dynamic import so knip can see it.
options.why: That adds code, which a deletions-only routine may never do.

follow.say: Make a tiny app with one used function, one unused export, one unused file, and a widget loaded by name.
Run the finder. knip lists suspects: two files and one export.
follow.see:
Unused files (2)
src/legacyBanner.ts
src/widgets/chart.ts
Unused exports (1)
quotaPercent  src/quota.ts:2:14

follow.say: Write a simple verifier. For every candidate it searches the code for the name, and for files also for the folder name, so a dynamic import is found.
follow.do:
cat > ../verify.sh <<'EOF'
# Prove or drop every knip candidate. Anything that might still be used is dropped.
report=$(npx -y knip@5 --no-progress --reporter json 2>/dev/null)
for file in $(echo "$report" | jq -r '.files[]'); do
  name=$(basename "$file" .ts); folder=$(basename "$(dirname "$file")")
  hits=$(grep -rn --include='*.ts' -e "$name" -e "$folder/" src | grep -v "^$file:")
  if [ -n "$hits" ]; then echo "DROP    $file  (maybe used: $(echo "$hits" | head -1 | cut -c1-60))"; else echo "PROVEN  $file"; fi
done
for item in $(echo "$report" | jq -r '.issues[] | .file as $f | .exports[] | "\($f):\(.name)"'); do
  file=${item%%:*}; name=${item#*:}
  hits=$(grep -rnw --include='*.ts' "$name" src | grep -v "^$file:")
  if [ -n "$hits" ]; then echo "DROP    $name in $file"; else echo "PROVEN  $name in $file"; fi
done
EOF
bash ../verify.sh
follow.see:
PROVEN  src/legacyBanner.ts
DROP    src/widgets/chart.ts  (maybe used: src/index.ts:3:const loadWidget = (name: string) => import(`)
PROVEN  quotaPercent in src/quota.ts

lab.build: Be the one writer. Delete only the two PROVEN items: the file src/legacyBanner.ts and the export quotaPercent in src/quota.ts. Run node src/index.ts to check the app still works. Then add a knip.json that ignores src/widgets/** so the dropped widget is not proposed again next week, and run knip once more.
checks: npx -y knip@5 --no-progress prints nothing after your knip.json.
Your change only removes lines and files, apart from the new knip.json: no code was added.

solution.text:
rm src/legacyBanner.ts
sed -i.bak '/quotaPercent/d' src/quota.ts && rm src/quota.ts.bak
node src/index.ts                       # the app still runs
echo '{ "ignore": ["src/widgets/**"] }' > knip.json
npx -y knip@5 --no-progress             # nothing left to report

lab.fix: A teammate wants the routine to be faster, so they delete everything knip reports without running the verifier. Do the same in a copy of the app, then run node src/index.ts: the import of the widget fails. Explain why the verifier's rule is "drop when unsure" and not "delete when unsure".
explain: Why are there many readers but only one writer?
Why is knip a good finder but a bad judge?
Why does a dropped candidate cost nothing, while a wrong deletion costs a lot?
lab.done: Only proven items are gone, the app runs, and the dropped widget is still there and no longer reported.

check.q: Why does a code-health routine use many verifiers but only one writer?

options.text: Reading in parallel is safe and fast, but two writers in one codebase step on each other
options.why: Verifiers cannot change anything, so many can run at once. Changes come from one session, in one small PR.

options.text: Writers are more expensive models than verifiers
options.why: The models may differ, but the rule is about safety and reviewability, not price.

options.text: GitHub allows only one bot commit per PR
options.why: There is no such limit. The rule is our choice.

check.q: A verifier is not sure whether an export is used, because a config file names a component by string. What happens to it?

options.text: The writer deletes it, and CI will catch a mistake
options.why: A string reference may only fail at run time, after CI is green. That is the case the verifier exists for.

options.text: It is deleted only if it is under 10 lines
options.why: Size does not matter. Proof does.

options.text: It is dropped from this week's list and stays in the code
options.why: Anything unsure is dropped. It costs nothing to keep it one more week.

check.q: The test-gap routine writes a test that passes on clean code and also passes on its planted bug. Is the test kept?

options.why: Coverage alone does not show that a test catches bugs.

options.text: No, because it did not catch the bug it was written for
options.why: A test is kept only if it fails on its planted bug and passes on clean code.

options.text: Only if a reviewer likes it
options.why: The keep rule is mechanical, before any reviewer sees the PR.

p: fe-dead-code adds knip to frontend as a pinned devDependency with frontend/knip.json and the script knip --reporter json; its charter is frontend/**, never add_code, Sonnet 5.5 at medium, a lite Spot VM, schedule 17 4 * * 0-4, at most 10 items per PR, and verify, check-types and build must pass. The BE remover adds a [tool.vulture] block to cloud/rhinoCloud/pyproject.toml (min_confidence 80, Django decorators ignored) and runs the cloud unit tests and makemigrations --check before done.

The stretch routines share the shape: test-gaps (harness/src/routines/test-gaps.ts, Meta's ACH roles, at most 5 tests, paths limited to test folders), duplicates (harness/src/routines/duplicates.ts, jscpd and pylint duplicate-code, one merge a week), and the security fixer (orchestrator/src/triggers/security-findings.ts, Dependabot alerts and Vanta findings with a fixed version, proven with trivy before and after, owner from DevOps).

tickets.why: The FE dead-code remover: knip candidates, verifiers, one writer, at most 10 items.
The BE dead-code remover with vulture and Django's hidden usage.
The test-gap routine: plant a bug, filter it, keep a test only if it catches it.
The weekly duplicates sweep: one merge proposal with no behaviour change.
The security fixer: bumps for findings with a fixed release, proven by a scan.

words.plain: A tool, such as knip or vulture, that lists candidates. Its list is suspects, not facts.
A read-only helper session that proves a candidate or drops it.
A tool that lists unused files, exports and dependencies in a JavaScript or TypeScript project.
A small bug planted on purpose, to check whether a test catches it.

review.q: From memory: the shape every code-health routine shares.
review.a: A finder lists candidates; read-only verifiers prove or drop each one; one writer makes a small change; the PR shows the proof.

review.q: Name three places where frontend usage hides from knip.
review.a: Dynamic imports built from strings, string references in config, stories, e2e page objects, and exports of the shared @r/libs package.

remember: A finder's list is suspects: verifiers prove or drop each one, and one writer removes only what is proven, in a PR small enough to approve in minutes.
